<reason>B (PRO) kept the debate anchored on the overwhelming mass of mandatory charges — static service, delivery, and ticket fees that are fully knowable once address/seat are entered yet deliberately withheld until payment — and A never dislodged that core. B's Q2 jiu-jitsu (blended sticker = true total visible early = goal achieved) neutralized A's best predicted-consequence argument, and B's closing demolition of A4.5's concession ("where fees are knowable early, disclosure already happens") was both empirically apt and unanswered by A. A mounted a genuinely clever structural attack: the payment-surcharge and real-time surge examples were directly responsive and forced B into a "carve-out" admission for surge fees, which A exploited well in closing. But A's all-or-nothing textual attack is a proportionality loser — a rule covering every determined fee is not refuted because a sliver needs tailoring — and A's closing overstated the concession by claiming B admitted card surcharges are unknowable, when B5.2 argued the opposite (fixed published schedule). Both sides had one misdescription: B's premature "their answer round produced none" (chronologically false and contradicted by A2.1) and A's closing distortion of B5.2. A's clipped opening was a modest execution cost. B's path to victory stood more intact after the full exchange.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing attack on A4.5's concession — showing "disclosure already happens for knowable fees" is factually false (the $22→$31 static-fee ambush is the industry standard) and principle-conceding — collapsed A's remaining shelter; paired with B3.2's Q2 turning the blending prediction into goal-achievement, it left A defending only the surge-fee sliver.</best_rebuttal>
